Nor did Captain Sterling know that the treacherous Baron von Hess had already forced the kidnapped guide to reveal the location of the Sunken Temple, the first of the three trials on the path to Ixlan. He was also unaware that the Baron’s men were setting a trap at the Singing Falls, believing Sterling’s party to have been crushed in the rockslide two days prior. The enormous weight of the salvaged generator parts did not interfere with the Vagabond’s function, whether she was on the river, in the swamp, or crawling through the jungle, as she was designed to manage a much heavier load. Gus and Kip were so relieved to be clear of the gorge that they produced a harmonica and a set of spoons, striking up a jaunty tune as the mechanical crawler tramped along.

The recent earthquake had left a wide scar through the jungle, felling ancient trees, exposing veins of glittering quartz in the earth, and diverting the course of a small tributary. “Had the Vagabond been in that gorge when the quake struck,” said Jack, “she would be nothing more than a thousand tons of scrap metal by now.”

“Aye, then it’s a good thing we stopped to repair the main piston,” answered Professor Thorne. “Now we must find the Sunken Temple.”

“It’s to the east, along this new river, is it not?”

“Yes,” answered Jack. “Why would the Baron have gone this way?”

“He is a cunning man, Captain. He knows we would expect him to take the most direct route.”

“You believe he is trying to throw us off his trail?”

“It is my firm conviction that he still has the guide, Tecu, with him on his launch, and does not want us to interfere. In a secluded spot like the falls upriver, he can force the man to talk, and no one will ever know what became of him. Do you take my meaning?”

“That is precisely what I was thinking, Professor.”

At that moment, a magnificent jaguar, black as polished jet, leaped onto a high branch overlooking the trail. The beast stared with its luminous green eyes at the strange machine, let out a low growl, and began to slink away along the branch.

“What a magnificent creature!” ejaculated Jack. “A prize for any museum.”

“For those who can get near it.”

“I think we could snare him.”

“With the net cannon?”

“Yes; if I can get a clear shot.”

“Try it.”

“You take the controls.”

The professor seized the levers, increased the pressure to the articulated legs, and Jack took up his position at the pneumatic cannon on the foredeck. The jaguar was now bounding from tree to tree with incredible speed, and the Vagabond crashed after it through the undergrowth. A loud hiss arose from the hydraulic limbs and a splintering of wood from under its heavy metal feet. Fast as the jaguar was, it was no match for the determined stride of the machine, and the Vagabond gradually closed the distance.

“The beast is following the cliff’s edge,” said the professor. “He’s running out of room!”

“Hold her steady, Professor!” shouted Jack. “I’m nearly in range.”

The jaguar was heading for a narrow stone bridge that crossed a deep chasm; but, for some reason, it suddenly stopped and refused to cross. Professor Thorne, instead of following its path, aimed the Vagabond directly for the bridge. It was only when they were nearly upon it that Jack saw the jaguar had been wise. The bridge was a crumbling ruin.

“Reverse! Reverse!” he cried.

Thorne pulled the lever, but it was too late. The front legs of the Vagabond stepped onto the ancient stonework, and with a great groaning crack, the entire structure gave way. Down plunged the Vagabond into the chasm. There was a tremendous splash. A deep, swift river ran at the bottom of the gorge. The machine hit the water with terrible force, and the impact sent a wave crashing over the deck. A block of dislodged stone from the cliff face struck Jack a glancing blow and hurled him overboard into the churning water.

Scarcely had he hit the river when the heavy stone followed him down, and he was driven deep into the darkness. Pushed under by the current, he felt his lungs begin to burn. For an instant Jack was so disoriented he thought his end had come; then he gathered his wits, and realizing his position, he kicked hard for the surface. It was fortunate that he swam with the current, for he came up in a pocket of air under an overhang beside the half submerged machine. Had he gone the other way he certainly would have been lost. Clinging to a twisted pipe, he held on until he caught his breath, and then he pulled himself onto the canted deck.

No one knew what had happened to him until he entered the main cabin, where he found Gus and Kip with the professor.

“Good heavens, Jack! What happened to you?” asked Thorne.

“Knocked overboard by a piece of the bridge.”

“Och, laddie, why did ye no’ shout?” asked Gus.

“I had little time for pleasantries, Gus.”

“Ye’d best get into some dry clothes and have a dram o’ the good stuff,” advised the Scot; “or, by my word, it’s a jungle fever ye’ll be catching.”

Jack smiled and disappeared below. When he returned in a fresh uniform, he showed no ill effects from his perilous swim. He found his companions assessing the damage to their vessel.

“The only thing for it is to engage the river turbines,” said Jack. “Let her drift downstream and see where this river leads.”

This plan was adopted. The Vagabond, now acting as a boat, was caught by the swift current. As the machine floated into the center of the chasm Frank looked up. Mighty waterfalls cascaded down the mossy cliffs, vast ferns hung like green chandeliers, and strange, glowing fungi pulsed with a soft light. Everything presented a wild and beautiful scene, wholly untouched by man, and yet alive with the sounds of unseen creatures.

League after league was passed. Finally Professor Thorne made a new calculation, and referring to his chart, he said to his friends in the cabin: “By my reckoning, we must be very near the Singing Falls now.”

“Aye, but I’ve seen no sign of a good place to moor,” said Gus.

“Neither have I,” said Jack. “But the distance traveled proves we are close,” he persisted.

Gus was about to offer a retort when there came a yell from Kip, who was perched on the roof.

“Smoke ahead! I see smoke from a cookfire!”

Every one was startled. They scrambled up the ladder. Off to the left, around a bend in the river, they saw the source. As soon as Jack saw it he cried:

“It is Baron von Hess’s camp!”

The Baron’s steam launch was tied up in a secluded cove, and the tents of his encampment were pitched in a clearing just beyond a screen of thick jungle.

CHAPTER IV.

INTO THE SERPENT’S NEST.

The sight of the Baron’s camp so near sent a thrill of anticipation through the crew of the Vagabond. Not a man was visible among the tents, and Jack at once ordered the turbines cut. The Vagabond drifted silently into the shadow of the cliff face.

“Well,” said Professor Thorne, “there is the man we are after. Now what is your plan of action, Jack?”

“First I must learn if Tecu is in that camp.”

“How will you manage that?”

“I am going ashore alone to have a look.”

“That is a reckless venture.”

“Very true, sir; but one I must undertake.”

“Well, we will keep a close watch from here, and if we see you are in trouble, we will be ready to provide a distraction.”

“That is all I ask.”

And so saying, Jack armed himself with a silenced pistol and a long knife, and slipping over the side of the Vagabond, he swam for the shore. At some distance from the camp, he found a game trail in the rocks, which he could use to climb up to the clearing. The air in which the camp sat was still, but the jungle was buzzing with insects, and the sound of the falls was now a constant, thunderous roar. Jack made his way up to the edge of the clearing.

Jack made his way up to the edge of the clearing. He crouched low behind a thick-leafed fern, its fronds large enough to conceal a man, and peered through the humid air at the scene below. Two tents of heavy canvas were pitched near a smouldering cookfire, and a larger pavilion, no doubt the Baron’s own, stood slightly apart. Several rough-looking men, armed with rifles, were lounging about, their talk a low murmur beneath the ceaseless thunder of the distant falls.

Jack’s eyes scanned the entire encampment. He saw the Baron von Hess himself, a tall, imperious figure with a neatly trimmed beard, emerge from the main pavilion and give a sharp order to one of the men. Yet of Tecu, the native guide they had come to rescue, there was no sign. Jack’s gaze then fell upon a smaller tent, set back from the others near the dark wall of the jungle. A single, heavily armed guard stood before its flap, pacing a short, three-step beat. It was clear that this tent held a prisoner.

“That must be the place,” Jack muttered to himself.

He knew a direct assault was folly. He had to be certain. Deciding upon a course of greater risk, he began to circle the clearing, keeping to the deep shadows where the jungle met the camp. He moved with the silence of a jaguar, his feet making no sound upon the damp earth. The air was thick with the scent of woodsmoke and decay. As he drew nearer the guarded tent, he was able to make out the voices of two of the mercenaries who were cleaning their rifles nearby.

“The Baron is getting impatient,” said one, a burly man with a scarred face. “He wants the prisoner to talk before we reach the falls.”

“He will not talk,” answered the other. “His kind is stubborn. But it makes no matter. The Baron has the map. The guide was only to make the journey quicker.”

“What will become of him, then?”

“The Baron said that once we have the Sun Stone, the guide is of no more use to us than a dead snake. He can be left for the jungle to claim.”

Jack’s blood ran cold at these callous words. He now knew for a certainty that Tecu was in the tent, and that his life was in grave peril. He had to act, and act quickly. He crept closer still, his eyes fixed on the lone sentry. He was so intent on his purpose that he failed to notice a thick, mottled serpent coiled on a low-hanging branch just above his path. As he passed under it, the creature, disturbed by his movement, dropped from its perch.

It landed with a soft thud directly in front of him. Jack froze, his heart in his throat. The snake raised its head, its forked tongue tasting the air. Its beady eyes fixed upon him. A single cry, a single sudden movement, would bring the entire camp down upon him. The sentry was less than twenty feet away, his back momentarily turned. With a motion too quick for the eye to follow, Jack’s hand shot out, his long knife flashing in the dim light. The blade pinned the serpent’s head to the ground, severing its spine in an instant. The body thrashed for a moment, and then was still.

Breathing a quiet sigh of relief, Jack did not linger. He had the information he needed. He retraced his steps with the same ghostly silence, slid back down the game trail, and swam through the cool water to the waiting Vagabond. He climbed aboard, water streaming from his clothes.

“Well?” asked Professor Thorne, his face etched with worry. “What did you discover?”

“Tecu is there,” Jack reported, his voice low and grim. “They have him in a guarded tent, and they mean to kill him once they find what they are looking for.”

“What are they lookin’ for?” asked Gus, wiping a grease-stained hand on a rag.

“Something called the Sun Stone. They say the Baron already has a map, and that Tecu is now expendable.”

“Then we have no time to lose!” ejaculated the Professor. “We must formulate a rescue.”

“My thoughts exactly, sir,” answered Jack. “Their camp is alert, but they are overconfident. The roar of the falls will help us. I propose a plan. Gus, you and Kip will create a diversion. I saw a place upstream where the cliff is unstable. If you could dislodge some of those boulders, it would sound like a landslide and draw their attention.”

“Aye, I can manage that,” said Gus, a determined glint in his eye. “A bit of well-placed leverage is all it will take.”

“While they are distracted,” Jack continued, “the professor and I will slip into the camp, free Tecu, and bring him back here. We must move under the cover of darkness.”

“It is a sound plan, Jack,” agreed the Professor, “though fraught with danger.”

“Every moment we delay, Tecu’s life hangs by a finer thread,” Jack insisted. “We will set out as soon as the moon is down.”

And so it was decided. They spent the next few hours making preparations. Jack cleaned and reloaded his silenced pistol. Professor Thorne gathered a small satchel of his own peculiar devices, including a small flask of a potent chemical and a compact galvanic battery. Gus and Kip, meanwhile, took the Vagabond’s small dinghy and rowed silently upstream to the place Jack had indicated. The great machine itself was left moored in the deep shadow of an overhanging cliff, perfectly hidden from view. The jungle night fell like a black curtain, and the only light came from the strange, pulsing fungi on the cavern walls and the distant flicker of the Baron’s campfire. The roar of the Singing Falls was a constant, deep-throated presence, a fitting symphony for the dangerous work ahead.

CHAPTER V.

A DARING RESCUE

When the last sliver of the moon had vanished behind the chasm’s high walls, Jack and Professor Thorne slipped over the side of the Vagabond and into the dark river. They swam to the shore and, cloaked in the immense darkness, made their way back up the game trail to the edge of the jungle. From their vantage point they could see the camp. Most of the mercenaries were now asleep, but two sentries still patrolled the perimeter, and the guard at Tecu’s tent remained as vigilant as ever.

Jack gave a low whistle, the signal they had agreed upon. Far upstream, there was a deep, grating sound, followed by a tremendous crash. A cascade of rocks and earth thundered down the cliff face, splashing into the river with a mighty roar that for a moment drowned out even the falls.

Immediately the camp was thrown into a state of alarm. Shouts of surprise and confusion rang out.

“What was that?”

“Landslide! Upstream!”

The Baron von Hess appeared from his pavilion, shouting orders. “Two of you, take the launch and investigate! The rest of you, secure the camp! Look sharp, now!”

As most of the men, including the Baron himself, rushed toward the riverbank to peer into the darkness upstream, Jack saw his opportunity. “Now, Professor!” he whispered.

The two of them darted from the cover of the jungle and raced across the open ground toward the prisoner’s tent. The remaining sentry, his attention diverted by the commotion, had taken a few steps away from his post to get a better view. He did not see them coming until it was too late. Before he could even cry out, Jack was upon him. There was a brief, silent struggle in the shadows, and the guard slumped to the ground, unconscious but alive. Jack had no desire to take a life if it could be avoided.

Professor Thorne stood watch, his hand inside his satchel, while Jack moved to the tent. With a single, swift slash of his knife, he cut a long slit in the rear of the canvas. He slipped inside.

The interior was pitch dark, and smelled of damp earth and fear. Jack’s eyes, accustomed to the gloom, soon made out a figure lying on a pile of straw. It was Tecu, his hands and feet bound with thick rope, and a foul gag stuffed in his mouth. The native’s eyes widened in the darkness as Jack knelt beside him, but he made no sound.

“I am a friend,” Jack whispered, his voice barely audible. “Do not be afraid. We are getting you out of here.”

He quickly and expertly sawed through the ropes with his knife. As soon as Tecu’s hands were free, the man tore the gag from his own mouth, gasping for air. He was weak and his limbs were stiff, but his eyes burned with a fire of defiance and gratitude.

“They seek the Sun Stone,” Tecu breathed, his voice a hoarse rasp. “You must not let them reach the sacred city.”

“First, we must get you to safety,” Jack replied. “Can you walk?”

“I can,” the native affirmed, struggling to his feet.

Just as they were about to exit through the slit in the canvas, a shadow fell across the tent’s main entrance. Another guard, drawn by some sixth sense of trouble, had come to check the post. He peered into the darkness, his rifle at the ready.

“Henri? Is all well?” he called out.

Professor Thorne, who stood flattened against the side of the tent, knew they were discovered. Before the guard could raise the alarm, the professor stepped out of the shadow. “Pardon me, my good man,” he said in a calm, academic voice. “I believe you have dropped this.”

The guard turned, bewildered, to see the elderly man holding out a small, shining object. As his eyes focused on it, the professor squeezed a bulb connected to the device. A brilliant, silent flash of white light, brighter than lightning, erupted from the object, straight into the guard’s face. The man gave a choked cry and staggered backward, clutching his eyes and completely blinded. He stumbled and fell, his rifle clattering on the rocks.

“Quickly now!” urged the Professor. “That will not hold him for long!”

Jack helped the unsteady Tecu out of the tent, and the three of them plunged back into the dark jungle just as the first shouts of discovery were raised from the camp.

“The prisoner is gone! He’s escaped!”

Gunshots cracked through the night air, the bullets whistling past them and thudding into the trees. The chase was on. The entire camp was now in an uproar, a hornet’s nest stirred to fury. Men with lanterns and rifles began fanning out, crashing through the undergrowth.

“This way!” Tecu hissed, taking the lead.

Despite his weakness, the native moved through the jungle with an uncanny skill. He seemed to know every path, every vine, every rock. He led them not back the way they had come, but along a winding, treacherous trail that clung to the side of the chasm. Behind them, the lights of their pursuers bobbed and weaved through the trees, getting closer. The Baron’s angry voice could be heard, urging his men on.

“They must not escape! A thousand florins to the man who brings me the guide!”

They scrambled over moss-slicked rocks and ducked under low-hanging vines thick as a man’s arm. They reached a deep fissure in the path, spanned only by a single, ancient vine bridge.

“It will hold,” Tecu assured them, and without hesitation, he ran across.

Jack followed, but as the Professor, who was less nimble, began to cross, a bullet splintered the rock near his hand. He flinched and nearly lost his footing, swaying precariously over the dark abyss. Jack, having reached the other side, turned and reached back for him.

“I have you, Professor!” he cried, grabbing his mentor’s arm and pulling him the rest of the way to safety. As soon as they were across, Jack drew his knife and with two quick slashes, severed the vine bridge. It fell away into the chasm, cutting off the most direct path of pursuit. They could hear the curses of the Baron’s men from the other side.

They had bought themselves precious time. They continued their desperate flight, sliding down a steep, muddy bank and finally reaching the river’s edge. In the distance, they saw the small, dark shape of the dinghy pulling up to the shore. Gus and Kip had returned.

“Over here!” Jack yelled.

They all scrambled into the small boat, nearly swamping it. Gus and Kip rowed with all their might, pulling for the deep shadow where the Vagabond was hidden. Bullets from the remaining pursuers on the riverbank began to splash in the water around them, sending up little fountains in the darkness.

“They’re aboard!” Kip shouted, as they reached the side of the larger vessel.

One by one they clambered up the ladder to the deck of the Vagabond. Jack was the last one aboard.

“Gus, the river turbines! Full power!” he commanded.

Gus leaped to the controls. With a deep hum that vibrated through the hull, the powerful turbines engaged, catching the swift current. The Vagabond shuddered and then began to move, pulling away from the shore and into the main channel of the subterranean river. It gathered speed quickly, leaving the Baron’s camp and the angry shouts of his men behind them in the echoing darkness. For the moment, they were safe.

CHAPTER VI.

THE BARON’S FURY

Aboard the Vagabond, a palpable sense of relief settled over the small crew. They had bearded the lion in his den and come away with their prize. Kip brought Tecu a mug of fresh water and some dried meat, which the native devoured gratefully. Professor Thorne examined the man’s wrists and ankles, which were raw from the ropes, and applied a soothing salve from his medical kit.

“We are in your debt,” Tecu said, his voice stronger now. He looked at Jack with deep respect. “You risked everything for me. My people will not forget this.”

“The Baron mentioned a Sun Stone,” said Jack. “And a map. What is his purpose in this forbidden place?”

Tecu’s face grew grave. “The Sun Stone is not a mere jewel,” he explained. “It is a legacy from the ancestors, a source of great energy. It provides light and warmth for our city, which lies hidden in a valley beyond the Singing Falls. It is the heart of our people. The Baron is a thief who seeks to steal our heart for his own greedy purposes. He tortured me for the way, but I did not speak. However, I fear he has another source of information.”

“The map,” Professor Thorne mused, his scientific curiosity piqued. “He must have plundered it from some earlier, failed expedition. An artifact that provides light and warmth! It sounds like a technology far beyond our own. Fascinating!”

“Fascinating or not, if this Baron gets his hands on it, it means trouble,” said Gus, ever the pragmatist. “We’ve made an enemy of him, that’s for certain.”

Gus’s words were truer than he knew. Back at the encampment, Baron von Hess was in a state of black rage. The escape of his prisoner, right from under his nose, was an insult he could not bear. He paced back and forth before the smouldering fire like a caged tiger, his men keeping a wary distance.

“Fools! Incompetents!” he roared, his voice echoing off the jungle walls. He stopped before the two guards who had been closest to the escape, the one Jack had knocked out and the one the Professor had blinded. The latter was still blinking, his vision a painful blur.

“You let them slip away!” the Baron snarled. “You are not fit to be called men!” Without another word, he drew his pistol and shot both of them where they stood. The other mercenaries looked on in cold silence, their faces impassive. The Baron was not a man to be crossed.

He turned to his second in command, a lean, cruel-faced man named Schmidt. “They have the guide,” the Baron said, his voice now a low, dangerous hiss. “But they do not know that the map is the true key. We will reach the falls before them. Ready the launch. We will pursue them at once. Their strange machine cannot hide from me in this river.”

“At once, Herr Baron,” Schmidt replied with a crisp salute.

Within minutes, the Baron’s sleek steam launch, its engine fired and hissing, pulled away from the shore. It was faster and more powerful than the Vagabond in a straight chase, built for speed on open water. A powerful searchlight was mounted on its bow, and the Baron himself stood behind it, sweeping the beam across the dark water ahead.

Meanwhile, on the Vagabond, our heroes were making their way down the winding river. The chasm had widened, and the current grew swifter. The constant roar of the Singing Falls was now deafeningly loud, a sure sign they were drawing near.

It was Kip who saw it first. He was perched again on the roof of the cabin, his young eyes scanning the river behind them.

“A light!” he shouted, his voice high with alarm. “There’s a light behind us, and it’s coming fast!”

Jack and the Professor rushed out on deck. They looked back and saw it: a single, brilliant beam cutting a swath through the darkness, swinging back and forth and growing steadily larger.

A DARING RESCUE

When the last sliver of the moon had vanished behind the chasm’s high walls, Jack and Professor Thorne slipped over the side of the Vagabond and into the dark river. “This way!” Tecu hissed, taking the lead.

Despite his weakness, the native moved through the jungle with an uncanny skill. He seemed to know every path, every vine, every rock. He led them not back the way they had come, but along a winding, treacherous trail that clung to the side of the chasm. Behind them, the lights of their pursuers bobbed and weaved through the trees, getting closer. The Baron’s angry voice could be heard, urging his men on.

“They must not escape! A thousand florins to the man who brings me the guide!”

They scrambled over moss-slicked rocks and ducked under low-hanging vines thick as a man’s arm. They reached a deep fissure in the path, spanned only by a single, ancient vine bridge.

“It will hold,” Tecu assured them, and without hesitation, he ran across.

Jack followed, but as the Professor, who was less nimble, began to cross, a bullet splintered the rock near his hand. He flinched and nearly lost his footing, swaying precariously over the dark abyss. Jack, having reached the other side, turned and reached back for him.

“I have you, Professor!” he cried, grabbing his mentor’s arm and pulling him the rest of the way to safety. As soon as they were across, Jack drew his knife and with two quick slashes, severed the vine bridge. It fell away into the chasm, cutting off the most direct path of pursuit. They could hear the curses of the Baron’s men from the other side.
